defaultWrong: That did not address the cause, so the problem carries on.

actions.label: Rotate certificate
actions.hint: Issue and install a new one

incidents.title: Errors spiked right after the latest release
symptoms: Error rate jumped from about 0.2% to more than 7% within a minute.
Most failures are HTTP 500 from the application itself.
evidence: Traffic is normal and there are no infrastructure alerts.
incidents.fixText: Returned {env} to the previous build. Errors fall back to normal.

wrong.restart: Restarting loads the same broken code, so the errors come straight back.
wrong.scale: More replicas of a broken release just produce more errors.
wrong.fallback: The failing code is our own, not a dependency, so a fallback changes nothing.
wrong.rotate: Certificates and credentials are fine. The trouble started with the deploy.
wrong.wait: Errors keep burning the error budget. A bad release does not fix itself.

incidents.explanation: The last deploy introduced a defect. Everything else about the service was normal, and the timing lines up with the deploy.
incidents.lesson: When trouble starts right after a release, roll back first and investigate afterwards. Mitigate before you diagnose.

incidents.title: Pods keep restarting and memory keeps climbing
symptoms: Pods restart every few minutes with OOMKilled.
Requests fail briefly each time a pod dies.
evidence: Memory use grows about 40 MB per minute.
Traffic is normal and nothing was changed today.
incidents.fixText: Recycled the pods. Memory is back to normal for now, but the leak is still in the code.

wrong.rollback: No recent deploy changed anything, so the previous build leaks too. (Simulated: nothing was rolled back.)
wrong.scale: More replicas leak as well. They just run out of memory at different times.
wrong.fallback: A fallback does not stop pods running out of memory.
wrong.rotate: Credentials are not the problem here.
wrong.wait: The pods keep dying and every restart drops requests.

incidents.explanation: A slow memory leak makes pods hit their limit and get killed. Nothing external changed.
incidents.lesson: A restart is mitigation, not a fix. Schedule the real fix and add a memory alert so it does not page you again.

incidents.title: Traffic is four times normal and latency is climbing
symptoms: Requests per second are about 4x the usual level.
CPU is above 90% on every pod.
Latency is rising and some requests time out.
evidence: No deploys in the last two days.
Errors rise only because requests are queueing.
incidents.fixText: Added replicas. Load spreads out and latency drops.

wrong.rollback: Nothing changed in the code, so rolling back would not reduce the load. (Simulated: nothing was rolled back.)
wrong.restart: Restarting removes capacity at exactly the wrong moment.
wrong.fallback: Fallbacks help with failing dependencies, not with too much load.
wrong.rotate: This is not a certificate or credential problem.
wrong.wait: Load is not going away, and users are waiting while the budget burns.

incidents.explanation: Demand outgrew capacity. The pods themselves are healthy, they are just overloaded.
incidents.lesson: Match capacity to load. Autoscaling and regular load tests make this a non-event.

incidents.title: Checkout is failing because the payment provider is down
symptoms: Calls to the payments API time out after 5 seconds.
Only the checkout path fails; browsing works.
Our pods look healthy: CPU and memory are normal.
evidence: The provider's status page reports an incident.
No deploys and no traffic change.
incidents.fixText: Switched checkout to the fallback: orders are queued and confirmed later. Customers can check out again.

wrong.rollback: The failure is outside our code, so the previous build fails the same way. (Simulated: nothing was rolled back.)
wrong.restart: Restarting your pods does not bring the provider back.
wrong.scale: More replicas just make more doomed calls.
wrong.rotate: Our credentials are fine. The provider is the one that is down.
wrong.wait: Customers cannot pay while you wait. A fallback lets them keep buying.

incidents.explanation: A third party failed. Our own service was healthy but depended on it.
incidents.lesson: Design for dependencies failing: timeouts, circuit breakers and fallbacks turn an outage into a degraded service.

incidents.title: Browsers reject the site: the TLS certificate expired
symptoms: Browsers show a security warning and refuse to connect.
Every external request fails the TLS handshake.
evidence: The certificate expired a few minutes ago.
No deploys and no config changes.
incidents.fixText: Issued and installed a new certificate. Handshakes succeed again.

wrong.rollback: The previous build has the same expired certificate. (Simulated: nothing was rolled back.)
wrong.restart: Restarting reloads the same expired certificate.
wrong.scale: More replicas present the same expired certificate.
wrong.fallback: No dependency failed. The certificate itself is invalid.
wrong.wait: Certificates do not renew themselves once they have expired.

incidents.explanation: The certificate reached its expiry date. The application and infrastructure were otherwise fine.
incidents.lesson: Automate certificate renewal and alert weeks before expiry, not minutes after.
